newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: GP Batteries to attack world market.
newsitem.headline: GP Batteries to attack world market.

text.p: GP Batteries International Ltd, Singapore-listed subsidiary of Hong Kong Gold Peak Industries (Holdings) Ltd, is planning an assault on world markets, a senior company official said on Wednesday.
"We have planned a two-pronged attack on the world (battery) markets," chairman Andrew Ng said at a press conference.
"Efforts in regional and emerging markets where big names are not so strong, we try to promote traditional batteries," Ng said, identifying China, Eastern Europe and Russia as examples.
In developed countries, he said the company's target was to sell rechargable batteries and higher-end products like nickel metal hydride rechargable batteries.
"We will focus in these two directions to strengthen markets where we already have some success, like in China...to protect the headstart we had," Ng said.
Ng said he estimated the world's primary battery market was growing at 4-5 percent a year and rechargable battery market at 12-13 percent.
GP Batteries now has nine percent of the world's market share for rechargable batteries compared to zero 5-6 years ago.
In the year ended March 1996, GP reported a 15.4 percent increase in profits to Singapore $20.7 million (US$14.7 million) on a turnover of S$309.5 million.
Ng said the company now concentrated on quality rather than high turnover "because looking for growth without quality, if there is a slow down, quality is ultimately more important".
"We are planning for a steady, monotonous progression and taking a long-term view because of the high investment," he said, adding that newcomers found it difficult to get into the market.

He said there was a period when turnover was more crucial than profit to the company. That was when it was smaller and had to focus on rapid growth to gain credibilty and recognition. However, this changed as it grew to its present size.

Ng said that by the end of the year, GP Batteries would be the largest zinc carbon battery maker in China after a major factory expansion there, which would see production rise by 25 to 30 percent from 40 million per month currently.
It now accounts for more than half the world's production of this type of battery.
Ng said rechargable batteries, used mainly in communications, computers and camcorders, accounted for half the company's turnover.
Specialty batteries used in toys, watches and other consumer electronic devices accounted for the other half.
"Our two businesses are complimentary. One protects the other from business fluctuations," Ng said.
He said rechargable batteries were mostly purchased by manufacturers and demand for them tended to fluctuate with product developments.
Ng said the company intended to "proceed gradually" in countries like Russia, where despite having great market potential, payment collection was difficult.
